Abstract path: SATCOM weakness -> shipboard foothold -> navigation-system reachability -> payload persistence -> AIS visual trigger -> ECDIS manipulation
Main interpretation: A communication-system CVE provides the initial access or reconnaissance point, but the cyber-physical consequence appears only after the path reaches the navigation environment.
Comments for feasibility analysis: Useful for showing that SATCOM vulnerabilities are not only communication risks. They may become entry points toward bridge systems, especially when segmentation, maintenance access, or credential hygiene is weak.

Abstract path: Gateway CVE -> IT/OT bridge -> navigation-data path -> false AIS or NMEA influence -> operator or automation response
Main interpretation: A router, serial gateway, wireless access point, or shipboard data gateway can turn a generic infrastructure CVE into a maritime cyber-physical risk.
Comments for feasibility analysis: This scenario emphasizes topology. The same vulnerability may have low impact in isolation but high impact if the affected device connects communication, navigation, maintenance, or OT networks.

Abstract path: Crafted navigation data -> parser weakness -> process crash or compromise -> display or data-path manipulation -> cyber-physical effect
Main interpretation: Navigation inputs such as AIS, GPS, NMEA 0183, and NMEA 2000 may be both the data source and the attack surface.
Comments for feasibility analysis: This path connects implementation-level CVEs with protocol-level weaknesses. Even without full compromise, crafted inputs may produce denial of service, misleading targets, false alerts, or abnormal ECDIS behavior.

Abstract path: Insecure update -> persistent modification -> dormant payload -> external AIS/radar trigger -> malicious action
Main interpretation: An insecure update or maintenance weakness can install a dormant component that is later activated through AIS or radar.
Comments for feasibility analysis: This is closest to the triggering model of Leite Junior et al. The CVE-enabled stage explains how the malicious component may be present; the AIS/ECDIS stage explains how it may be activated later.
